openingLine: Hello, I'm Ingrid. The hospital told me to come see you about taking my gallbladder out, after that business with my pancreas.

rounds.prompt: Her chart shows only high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and one record source failed to sync. What do you do next?

choices.text: Ask her to walk you through the hospital stay: where, when, how serious, and what they tested
choices.feedback: The admission lives in the unsynced Quillhaven source, so only she can tell you it was mild, that the bile duct MRI was clear, and when it happened.
choices.patientCue: Let me be exact. About four weeks ago at Quillhaven, for three days. They said it was mild, I never went to the ICU, and before I went home they did an MRI of my bile ducts and said no stones were stuck.

choices.text: Tell her the chart shows no recent admission, so there must be a mix up
choices.feedback: A failed source sync means missing data, not normal data, so the chart cannot overrule her account.
choices.patientCue: Well, I was there for three days about four weeks ago, at Quillhaven. I'm not mixed up about that.

choices.text: Ask where the pain was back then and what it felt like
choices.feedback: The classic pain story is useful, but it does not fill the chart gap about how severe the episode was and whether the bile duct was cleared.
choices.patientCue: Well, it was in the upper middle of my belly, boring straight through to my back. A terrible, steady pain, a ten. Nothing now.

choices.text: Wait for the Quillhaven records to sync before taking a history
choices.feedback: The source may never sync, and the patient in front of you is the best available record.
choices.patientCue: Well, I'm right here. I left my notebook on the kitchen table, which annoys me, but I can tell you what happened.

rounds.prompt: She says she feels fine today. What do you do next?

choices.text: Ask about her last menstrual period
choices.feedback: At 68 she is postmenopausal, and this does not screen for complications since discharge.
choices.patientCue: Well, I'm long past menopause.

choices.text: Ask whether she has had any pain, nausea or vomiting since she got home
choices.feedback: Confirming she is pain free helps, but fever, dark urine and pale stools are what flag cholangitis or a retained duct stone.
choices.patientCue: Today it's zero. I threw up a lot in the hospital, but none since I got home.

choices.text: Ask about fever, dark urine or pale stools since discharge
choices.feedback: No fever, dark urine or pale stools makes cholangitis or a retained bile duct stone unlikely.
choices.patientCue: No fevers since I got home. My urine hasn't been dark, and my bowels are normal. No pale stools.

choices.text: Tell her she sounds well and move straight to scheduling
choices.feedback: Skipping the post discharge review risks missing a complication that would change the plan.
choices.patientCue: Well, I do want it on the calendar. But don't you want to know how I've been?

rounds.prompt: The chart lists lisinopril, atorvastatin and a penicillin allergy. What do you do next?

choices.text: Ask everything she takes, including over the counter pills, and exactly what happened with penicillin
choices.feedback: This uncovers the self started aspirin that is in no chart and shows the penicillin reaction was a remote mild rash, so cefazolin is fine.
choices.patientCue: Lisinopril in the morning and atorvastatin at night. I also take a baby aspirin most days on my own, nobody prescribed it. Penicillin gave me an itchy red rash on my arms and chest when I was about thirty, no swelling, no trouble breathing.

choices.text: Confirm the two listed prescriptions and the penicillin allergy as charted
choices.feedback: Reading back the chart confirms what is listed but misses the unlisted aspirin and the nature of the penicillin reaction.
choices.patientCue: Well, yes. Lisinopril in the morning and atorvastatin at night. And yes, penicillin.

choices.text: Ask whether she has ever had surgery
choices.feedback: Surgical history matters, but it does not address the medication and allergy risks flagged in the chart.
choices.patientCue: I've never had surgery. I had a colonoscopy at sixty and it was fine.

choices.text: Write that she must avoid all beta lactam antibiotics, without asking more
choices.feedback: An uncharacterized label leads to needlessly worse prophylaxis when a remote mild rash still allows cefazolin.
choices.patientCue: Say that again in plain English, please. I did numbers, not medicine.

rounds.prompt: You want to confirm what caused the pancreatitis. What do you do next?

choices.text: Tell her it was probably from drinking
choices.feedback: Assuming alcohol without asking is inaccurate and alienating, and her history points to stones.
choices.patientCue: Well, I hardly drink. Maybe a glass of wine at a wedding. They asked me about that a lot in the hospital too.

choices.text: Ask whether anyone in the family has had gallstones
choices.feedback: Family history supports a stone cause, but alcohol, the other common cause, still has to be asked about.
choices.patientCue: My sister had gallstones.

choices.text: Ask what she ate this morning
choices.feedback: Her last meal matters for anesthesia on the day of surgery, not for the cause of last month's pancreatitis.
choices.patientCue: Toast and coffee at eight this morning.

choices.text: Ask calmly about alcohol and smoking, and about gallstones in the family
choices.feedback: Minimal alcohol and a sister with gallstones make stones the clear cause and rule out the other common culprit.
choices.patientCue: I never smoked. Maybe a glass of wine at a wedding, that's it. And my sister had gallstones.

rounds.prompt: She is pain free and cooperative. What do you do next?

choices.text: Palpate the abdomen
choices.feedback: A soft abdomen without a mass helps exclude a collection, but you also need vitals, a jaundice check and a Murphy sign.
choices.patientCue: No, that's all fine now.

choices.text: Check vitals, look for jaundice, then palpate the abdomen including a Murphy sign
choices.feedback: Normal vitals, no jaundice, a soft abdomen and a negative Murphy sign confirm recovery and no ongoing gallbladder inflammation.
choices.patientCue: Go ahead. No, that's all fine now. No, that doesn't hurt.

finding.label: Vitals and abdominal exam
finding.text: Vitals: Temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 72, blood pressure 132/80, respiratory rate 14, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Weight 81 kg. General: Well appearing. No jaundice, no scleral icterus. Palpation: Soft and nontender. No mass. Murphy: Negative Murphy sign.

choices.text: Press on McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant
choices.feedback: McBurney's point screens for appendicitis, which is not the question here.
choices.patientCue: No.

finding.label: McBurney point
finding.text: Nontender in the right lower quadrant.

choices.text: Perform a pelvic exam
choices.feedback: A pelvic exam adds nothing for a postmenopausal woman recovering from gallstone pancreatitis.
choices.patientCue: Well, I'm long past menopause. Is that really needed for this?

rounds.prompt: Her exam is benign. What do you order?

choices.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
choices.feedback: After mild pancreatitis that has resolved, CT adds radiation without changing the plan, and it shows the stones poorly.
choices.patientCue: I'd rather not have a scan with radiation, unless I need it.

finding.label: CT abdomen and pelvis
finding.text: No peripancreatic collection or necrosis. Gallstones not well seen.

choices.text: Lipase only, to confirm the pancreatitis has resolved
choices.feedback: A normal lipase confirms resolution, but you still need liver tests to exclude a retained duct stone and an ultrasound to show the stones.
choices.patientCue: Fine.

choices.text: CBC, BMP, liver tests, lipase and a right upper quadrant ultrasound
choices.feedback: Normal liver tests with a 5 mm duct exclude a retained stone, lipase confirms resolution, BMP checks kidneys, calcium and glucose, and ultrasound shows the stones.
choices.patientCue: Fine. Another scan? Alright, as long as it's not the radiation kind.

finding.label: Labs and ultrasound
finding.text: CBC: White count 6.9, hemoglobin 13.4, platelets 245. Normal. BMP: Sodium 140, potassium 4.4, creatinine 0.9, glucose 102, calcium 9.4. Normal. LFTs: Total bilirubin 0.7, alkaline phosphatase 88, AST 24, ALT 21. Normal: no sign of a retained bile duct stone. Lipase: Lipase 42 (normal). Ultrasound: Multiple small gallstones and sludge. Gallbladder wall 3 mm, no pericholecystic fluid. Common bile duct 5 mm. Pancreas partly obscured by bowel gas, no peripancreatic fluid seen.

choices.text: Urinalysis and CRP
choices.feedback: Neither test addresses a retained duct stone, resolution of the pancreatitis, or the stones themselves.
choices.patientCue: Fine.

choices.text: Resolved mild gallstone pancreatitis, due for interval cholecystectomy
choices.feedback: Stones on ultrasound, minimal alcohol, normal calcium, a clear duct and a normal lipase define resolved mild gallstone pancreatitis needing the gallbladder out.
choices.patientCue: Well, that matches what the hospital said. I never want to go through that again.

choices.text: Retained common bile duct stone
choices.feedback: A clear bile duct MRI, normal liver tests, a 5 mm duct and no jaundice argue against a retained stone.
choices.patientCue: They told me no stones were stuck. That's what the MRI of my bile ducts was for.

choices.text: Gallstone disease
choices.feedback: Gallstones are present, but naming the prior pancreatitis explains why surgery should not be put off.
choices.patientCue: Well, the stones, yes. But it was my pancreas that put me in the hospital.

choices.text: Alcohol related pancreatitis
choices.feedback: She drinks a glass of wine at a wedding at most, and gallstones are clearly present.
choices.patientCue: I hardly drink. Maybe a glass of wine at a wedding. Please write that down correctly.

choices.text: ERCP to clear the bile duct first, then reassess
choices.feedback: With a clear MRI, normal liver tests and a 5 mm duct there is no duct stone to clear, so ERCP adds risk without benefit.
choices.patientCue: Say that again in plain English, please. The hospital said no stones were stuck.

choices.text: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy in about six months, once everything has fully settled
choices.feedback: Right operation, but waiting months leaves her at high risk of another attack; it should be done within weeks.
choices.patientCue: Six months? I don't want to go through that again. How soon can it actually be done?

choices.text: Low fat diet and observation, operating only if it happens again
choices.feedback: Without removing the gallbladder, recurrent pancreatitis and other stone events are common.
choices.patientCue: Well, I already stay away from fried food. I'd rather not wait for it to happen again.

choices.text: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy within the next few weeks, cefazolin prophylaxis, a decision on her aspirin, and request the Quillhaven records
choices.feedback: Prompt elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy prevents recurrence, cefazolin suits her mild remote rash, and the aspirin and missing records are handled before the OR.
choices.patientCue: Good. Put me on the calendar. How soon can it be done?

closingLine: Good. Put me on the calendar. I never want to go through that pain again, so the sooner the better.
